passage:
Vikas,

I'm writing this because last night, at eleven, we were both too tired and I did not want to say the wrong thing about the phone bill and the money for your brother. So I'm glad we stopped. Tonight, after dinner, when the dishes are done, can we sit down for half an hour? I want to tell you what I need: to know about money before it leaves our account, not after. And I want to hear your side fully, without me finishing your sentences. I know your family matters to you and I'm not asking you to pick. Maybe we can decide one small thing together, like a limit we both agree on, and look at it again next month. I'm not keeping a list of who did what. I just want us on the same side of the table. 🙂

Sunaina

qa.q: When does Sunaina ask Vikas to sit down and talk?
qa.a: Tonight, after dinner, when the dishes are done, for half an hour.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina stop the talk at eleven at night, and what does Sunaina hope for now?
qa.a: Sunaina was afraid of saying the wrong thing while both were tired, and hopes for a calmer talk where Sunaina states the need and hears Vikas's side fully.

qa.q: What would you advise Vikas to do when they sit down?
qa.a: Listen to the end, say what Vikas needs too, and agree one small next step, such as a limit they will look at again next month.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel when reading the line about the brother?
qa.a: Vikas might worry about being asked to choose between Sunaina and the family, so Sunaina's words about not asking Vikas to pick may ease that.

grounding: Shows a spouse choosing timing, stating a money need, promising to listen fully and proposing a next step instead of keeping score.

passage:
People ask how we stopped fighting about the weekends. We didn't stop. We changed how.

I'm Nitin. Pooja and I have been married two years. Every Sunday her parents came for lunch, and every Sunday I cooked and cleaned while everyone else talked. By evening I'd say something sharp, she'd list the times my family visited, and we'd both keep score till midnight.

One Tuesday, not a Sunday, I asked if we could talk after dinner, phones away. I said, "I feel invisible on Sundays. I need help in the kitchen, and one Sunday a month for just us." Then I stopped and let her talk. She said she felt torn between her parents and me, and was afraid of hurting them.

We agreed: her parents come twice a month, she and her father clear up, and the fourth Sunday is ours. We tried it for a month.

It's not perfect. It's much better.

qa.q: What did Nitin ask for when they talked on Tuesday?
qa.a: Nitin asked for help in the kitchen and one Sunday a month for just the two of them.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling on Sunday evenings before they changed things?
qa.a: Nitin felt invisible, resentful and tired, which came out as sharp remarks and scorekeeping.

qa.q: Which choices made the Tuesday talk work?
qa.a: Picking a calm time, stating needs with "I feel", listening fully and agreeing on a concrete next step instead of keeping score.

qa.q: How does Pooja experience the Sunday lunches?
qa.a: Pooja feels torn between her parents and Nitin and is afraid of hurting her parents.

grounding: Shows a spouse handling an in-law and chores disagreement by choosing a calm time, stating needs, listening and agreeing on a next step instead of keeping score.

passage:
I'm staying with my sister Avni and her husband Kishore while I study for exams, so I see a lot.

Last month Kishore's mother phoned to say she wanted to live with them after the winter. Kishore said yes on the call. Avni didn't say anything until the phone was down. Then she went very still and said, "Not now. We'll talk on Saturday morning." I thought she was avoiding it.

On Saturday they sat on the balcony with tea. I heard Avni say, "I love your mother. I need us to decide together, and I need my study room." Kishore listened without cutting in; he just nodded. Then he said he was worried about his mother being lonely.

It took an hour. They agreed his mother would come for two months first, and they would all talk again after.

I don't know if Avni was fully happy, but nobody slammed a door.

qa.q: For how long did they agree Kishore's mother would come first?
qa.a: They agreed his mother would come for two months first.

qa.q: What might Avni's stillness after the phone call suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Avni felt upset and hurt that Kishore agreed without her, but chose to wait for a calmer time instead of arguing immediately.

qa.q: What approach helped Avni and Kishore reach an agreement?
qa.a: Choosing a calm time, stating needs clearly, listening without cutting in and agreeing on a trial period as a next step.

qa.q: What is Kishore worried about in this disagreement?
qa.a: Kishore is worried about his mother being lonely.

grounding: Shows spouses handling an in-law disagreement by choosing timing, stating needs, listening fully and agreeing on a next step.
